Predicting the interaction between a target protein and a drug candidate is crucial in drug discovery, but simulating its fundamental quantum mechanical structure could previously only be applied to extremely small-scale systems due to limitations in computational scale. However, a recent study successfully and accurately simulated complex protein-ligand complexes consisting of over 12,000 atoms through "heterogeneous quantum-classical (HQC) computing," which combines quantum computers with classical supercomputers, drawing the attention of the global pharmaceutical and IT industries.
Utilizing two 156-qubit quantum processors (ibm_cleveland, ibm_kobe) and two supercomputers (Fugaku, Miyabi-G), the research successfully simulated the quantum chemistry of protein-ligand complexes consisting of more than 12,000 atoms. The HQC method matched the accuracy level of the classical coupled-cluster (CCSD) method in fragment energies, proving its practical, industrial-scale potential to drastically reduce the time and cost of the drug discovery pipeline.
Through this innovative workflow, the research team successfully simulated two giant protein-ligand complexes spanning dispersion- and electrostatics-dominated regimes (comprising 11,608 and 12,635 atoms, respectively). As a result, compared to previous state-of-the-art technologies, they achieved the feat of expanding the size of the simulatable system by more than 40 times and improving computational accuracy by up to 210 times. In particular, it is highly encouraging that the HQC method reached the high accuracy of the classical coupled-cluster (CCSD) level in fragment energy calculations.
The study, "Crossing the 12,000-atom barrier with heterogeneous quantum-classical supercomputing: quantum chemistry of protein-ligand complexes," published on the preprint repository arXiv, was conducted by a multinational joint research team. A joint team used two 156-qubit IBM Heron processors and three supercomputers to compute the electronic structure of protein-ligand complexes up to 12,635 atoms — the largest biologically meaningful molecules known to be modelled with quantum hardware.
## What was actually announced
On 5 May 2026, Cleveland Clinic, Japan's RIKEN and IBM announced that they had simulated the electronic structure of two protein-ligand complexes spanning 11,608 and 12,635 atoms — described as the largest known simulations of biologically meaningful molecules performed with quantum hardware.
The larger of the two systems is a complex built around trypsin, a digestive enzyme long used as a workhorse in structural biology. [1] The point of the exercise was not the enzyme itself but the size threshold: quantum chemistry calculations on quantum processors had previously been confined to small molecules, and the team reports roughly a 40-fold jump in system size over what the same method could handle six months earlier. The scale of the run is unusually well documented for a quantum-computing milestone. Sampling ran on two 156-qubit IBM Quantum Heron processors — ibm_cleveland, installed at Cleveland Clinic in Ohio, and ibm_kobe at RIKEN — using up to 94 qubits, executing 21,006 circuits over more than 239 hours and collecting about 3.0 billion measurement outcomes.
The classical half ran on Fugaku at RIKEN, Miyabi-G (operated by the University of Tokyo and the University of Tsukuba) and ROQUO, with the distributed linear-algebra kernels reported at 72.5% parallel efficiency. [1][4]

# Quantum leap: Largest ever protein model hits 12,635 atoms with 210x accuracy boost

Researchers at IBM, the Cleveland Clinic, and Japan's RIKEN research institute have used quantum computers in conjunction with two of the world's most powerful supercomputers to simulate a protein complex comprising 12,635 atoms. This achievement represents the largest biologically meaningful molecule ever modeled using quantum hardware, as announced at IBM's Think 2026 conference in Boston.

The simulation is approximately 40 times larger than the team's previous achievement six months earlier and constitutes a significant advancement toward the application of quantum-classical hybrid systems in drug discovery and biomedical research.

## Overview of computational approach

The research focused on trypsin, a digestive enzyme commonly used as a drug-interaction model, as well as a second protein-ligand complex. Classical supercomputers partitioned each molecule into computable fragments.

IBM's 156-qubit Heron processors, located at the Cleveland Clinic in the United States and RIKEN in Kobe, Japan, calculated the quantum-mechanical behavior of these fragments using up to 94 qubits and nearly 6,000 quantum operations per simulation segment.

The results were subsequently reassembled on classical systems, including RIKEN's Fugaku supercomputer and Miyabi-G, operated by the University of Tokyo and University of Tsukuba, to generate a complete molecular representation.

The computational framework, termed quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) by IBM, is a tightly coupled, closed-loop architecture in which quantum and classical processors exchange data iteratively rather than operate sequentially.

Each system addresses the aspects of the problem for which it is best suited. Quantum processors sample extensive electron configuration spaces that are intractable for classical methods, while supercomputers perform deterministic diagonalization and final assembly.

deepseek.snippet: Quantum computers just simulated a protein system with over 12,000 atoms, the largest biologically meaningful molecular simulation ever performed with quantum hardware. A research team used a hybrid workflow combining two quantum processors with two classical supercomputers to model protein-ligand complexes, which are the types of molecular interactions fundamental to drug discovery and structural biology. The approach is built on a divide-and-conquer strategy. Classical supercomputers first break large molecular systems into smaller fragments. Quantum processors then calculate the quantum-mechanical behaviors of those pieces, and classical systems reassemble the results into a complete molecular picture. Here is what makes this significant: The systems modeled were roughly 40 times larger than what quantum computers could handle just six months ago. Accuracy in a key step of the workflow improved by up to 210 times. For the first time in this type of calculation, the researchers explicitly included solvent molecules, adding a layer of realism that matters for practical applications. This matters because drug discovery depends on understanding how small molecules interact with proteins, and those interactions are governed by quantum mechanics. Classical methods either sacrifice accuracy for speed or become computationally impractical at meaningful scales. Quantum-centric approaches offer a path toward simulations that are both accurate and tractable. The results have not yet been peer-reviewed, and independent experts note that comparison to experimental benchmarks will be essential. The trajectory is clear: quantum hardware is reaching the scale where it can contribute to real chemical and biological problems.

# Google Quantum AI Shows 13,000× Speedup Over World’s Fastest Supercomputer in Physics Simulation
- [Google Quantum AI](https://app.thequantuminsider.com/investor/d3025120-665c-41f6-813a-d341d969979c/profile)’s 65-qubit processor performed a complex physics simulation 13,000 times faster than the Frontier supercomputer, marking measurable progress toward practical quantum advantage.

Google Quantum AI has reported a physics experiment that pushes quantum computing further into what researchers call the “beyond-classical” regime, where even the world’s most powerful supercomputers fail to keep up. The scale of chemistry simulations with quantum computing has increased dramatically in just the last few months. [In the latest milestone for the field](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01138), researchers from Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN, and IBM used a quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) framework to calculate the electronic structure of a pair of large protein-ligand complexes, reaching a scale of 12,635 atoms in the largest simulation.
The molecules were T4-Lysozyme, a protein from a family of proteins involved in the immune system degradation of peptidoglycans in bacterial membranes, and Trypsin, produced in the pancreas and used in digestion. The team simulated these proteins binding to molecules they interact with in nature and immersed in a liquid water solution, at scales of 11,608 atoms and 12,635 atoms respectively. Bringing together an international team of researchers from across the United States and Japan made it possible to develop the necessary algorithm and workflow enhancements to reach this milestone.

The initial Trp-cage result on which this new work builds relies on a technique called [wave function-based embedding](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.09321) (EWF), which fragments the calculation into computationally tractable pieces called “clusters.” Classical computers solve the simpler clusters. Then, a quantum computer uses a method called [sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD)](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/learning/en/courses/quantum-diagonalization-algorithms/sqd-overview) to solve the more complex clusters—those involving more entanglement between atoms in the miniprotein. The classical computers then stitch the molecule back together.

To model the proteins T4-Lysozyme and Trypsin, the team used up to 94 qubits across two quantum computers, ran 9,200 circuits for over 100 hours, and collected 1.3 billion measurement outcomes. That makes this work the most resource-intensive known QCSC execution for quantum chemistry to date.

keenable-realtime.snippet:
The scale of chemistry simulations with quantum computing has increased dramatically in just the last few months. [In the latest milestone for the field](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01138), researchers from Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN, and IBM used a quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) framework to calculate the electronic structure of a pair of large protein-ligand complexes, reaching a scale of 12,635 atoms in the largest simulation.
The molecules were T4-Lysozyme, a protein from a family of proteins involved in the immune system degradation of peptidoglycans in bacterial membranes, and Trypsin, produced in the pancreas and used in digestion. The team simulated these proteins binding to molecules they interact with in nature and immersed in a liquid water solution, at scales of 11,608 atoms and 12,635 atoms respectively. Bringing together an international team of researchers from across the United States and Japan made it possible to develop the necessary algorithm and workflow enhancements to reach this milestone.

The initial Trp-cage result on which this new work builds relies on a technique called [wave function-based embedding](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.09321) (EWF), which fragments the calculation into computationally tractable pieces called “clusters.” Classical computers solve the simpler clusters. Then, a quantum computer uses a method called [sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD)](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/learning/en/courses/quantum-diagonalization-algorithms/sqd-overview) to solve the more complex clusters—those involving more entanglement between atoms in the miniprotein. The classical computers then stitch the molecule back together.

To model the proteins T4-Lysozyme and Trypsin, the team used up to 94 qubits across two quantum computers, ran 9,200 circuits for over 100 hours, and collected 1.3 billion measurement outcomes. That makes this work the most resource-intensive known QCSC execution for quantum chemistry to date.

ultimate.snippet: We develop a workflow decomposing a molecule into fragments via quantum embedding and simulating them with a heterogeneous quantum-classical (HQC) method. ultimate.title: Quantum-centric supercomputing simulates 12,635-atom protein
ultimate.snippet:
The scale of chemistry simulations with quantum computing has increased dramatically in just the last few months. [In the latest milestone for the field](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01138), researchers from Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN, and IBM used a quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) framework to calculate the electronic structure of a pair of large protein-ligand complexes, reaching a scale of 12,635 atoms in the largest simulation.
The molecules were T4-Lysozyme, a protein from a family of proteins involved in the immune system degradation of peptidoglycans in bacterial membranes, and Trypsin, produced in the pancreas and used in digestion. The team simulated these proteins binding to molecules they interact with in nature and immersed in a liquid water solution, at scales of 11,608 atoms and 12,635 atoms respectively. Bringing together an international team of researchers from across the United States and Japan made it possible to develop the necessary algorithm and workflow enhancements to reach this milestone.

The initial Trp-cage result on which this new work builds relies on a technique called [wave function-based embedding](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.09321) (EWF), which fragments the calculation into computationally tractable pieces called “clusters.” Classical computers solve the simpler clusters. Then, a quantum computer uses a method called [sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD)](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/learning/en/courses/quantum-diagonalization-algorithms/sqd-overview) to solve the more complex clusters—those involving more entanglement between atoms in the miniprotein. The classical computers then stitch the molecule back together.

To model the proteins T4-Lysozyme and Trypsin, the team used up to 94 qubits across two quantum computers, ran 9,200 circuits for over 100 hours, and collected 1.3 billion measurement outcomes. That makes this work the most resource-intensive known QCSC execution for quantum chemistry to date.

ultimate.title: Quantum computers simulated their biggest molecule yet – with help

However, two quantum computers have now broken a simulation record – determining the properties of a molecule with 12,635 atoms – with some help from supercomputers.

A collaboration between researchers at the Cleveland Clinic in Ohio, the US tech firm IBM and the Japanese scientific institute RIKEN has instead turned to quantum computers, which “speak” quantum physics by default. They developed a [hybrid approach](https://newscientist.com/article/2486900-quantum-enhanced-supercomputers-are-starting-to-do-chemistry/) that combines quantum computers and conventional supercomputers and used it to simulate two unprecedentedly large molecules, with one about 40 times bigger than the past largest molecule simulated using a quantum computer.

The researchers used two IBM Heron quantum computers, one located at RIKEN and one at the Cleveland Clinic, and two supercomputers called Fugaku and Miyabi-G, which are among the most powerful in the world. For the molecules, the team chose two combinations of a protein and a small molecule, or “protein-ligand complexes”, that Merz says are well studied and popular as fundamental examples in biomedical sciences. The team also simulated them in a layer of water, bringing the results closer to mimicking how researchers work with the molecules in the lab.

ultimate.snippet:
A new hybrid workflow involving two IBM quantum computers and two powerful supercomputers has allowed researchers to model two protein–ligand complexes containing up to 12,635 atoms – the largest simulations of biologically meaningful structures ever done with quantum hardware. The team from Cleveland Clinic in the US, Riken in Japan and IBM revealed their results in a preprint that has not been peer reviewed yet.

The researchers tested their method on two classic protein–ligand pairs: the digestive enzyme trypsin bound to the inhibitor benzamidine and T4 lysozyme bound to *n*-butyl-benzene, a model system used to study how small molecules bind inside proteins. ‘Quantum computers are now capable of tackling chemically and biologically relevant molecular systems,’ says [Kenneth Merz](https://www.lerner.ccf.org/computational-medicine/merz/) from Cleveland Clinic and Michigan State University, US, who led the study. But this advancement didn’t come from quantum hardware alone. Instead, Merz and his colleagues split the task between different kinds of machines. First, classical supercomputers broke the large protein–ligand systems into smaller fragments. Then, IBM’s 156-qubit quantum processors calculated the quantum-mechanical behaviours of those pieces in tandem with two classical supercomputers. Finally, the results were put back together on classical systems to construct the full molecular picture.

ultimate.title: RIKEN, IBM And Cleveland Clinic Run Quantum Chemistry On 12,635-atom System
ultimate.snippet:
Researchers from [RIKEN](https://quantumzeitgeist.com/ibm-demonstration-quantum-12635-atom-protein/), [IBM](https://quantumzeitgeist.com/ibm-210x-accuracy-boost-12635-atom/) and Cleveland Clinic have completed the most resource-intensive heterogeneous quantum-classical ([HQC](https://quantumzeitgeist.com/nist-selects-florida-atlantic-universitys-hqc-algorithm-for-post-quantum-cryptography-standards/)) computation for quantum chemistry to date, simulating a 12,635-atom system. The workflow decomposed molecules into fragments and used up to 94 qubits on ibm_cleveland and ibm_kobe quantum processors, running 21,006 circuits for over 239 hours and collecting 3.0 x 10^9 measurement outcomes.
This work demonstrates a greater than 40-fold increase in system size and up to a 210-fold improvement in accuracy over previous methods, with HQC matching coupled-cluster (CCSD) accuracy in fragment energies. The team also presented the first HQC protein-ligand binding prediction using an automated workflow for large protein systems.

The simulation of two protein-ligand complexes, containing 11,608 and 12,635 atoms respectively, represents a new scale for heterogeneous quantum-classical (HQC) calculations in quantum chemistry. Fragment electronic configurations were sampled across two 156-qubit quantum processors, ibm_cleveland and ibm_kobe, to achieve this increased complexity. The team used optimized subspace diagonalization on supercomputers [Fugaku](https://quantumzeitgeist.com/ibm-riken-deploy-japans-first-quantum-system-two-linked-to-fugaku-supercomputer/), Miyabi-G and [ROQUO](https://quantumzeitgeist.com/nedo-funds-rikens-jhpc-quantum-gpu/) to compute fragment wavefunctions, a process that yielded 72.5% parallel efficiency through scalable distributed linear algebra kernels.

Quantum hardware handled the most complex parts of the calculation, while classical supercomputers stitched the results together. The quantum data was then processed using powerful classical systems, including Japan’s Fugaku supercomputer.

you.title: Why a 12,635-Atom Protein Simulation Still Needs Supercomputers
you.snippet:
The current study establishes a route for large protein-ligand systems and reports strong agreement for selected fragment energies. It does not report a prospective compound-selection campaign, blinded prediction, wet-lab validation, or a drug advanced because of the quantum calculation. That gap is ordinary in computational science.
It is also a clear view of how much classical machinery surrounds the quantum step. The arXiv preprint by Kenneth M. Merz Jr. and 23 coauthors, submitted on May 1, 2026, studies two familiar proteins: T4 lysozyme and trypsin. Each protein was modeled with a binding molecule and surrounding water. That fuller scene matters because proteins do their work in an environment. Water, charge, and the shape of a binding pocket affect how a molecule fits and how strongly it interacts. The larger trypsin system contained 12,635 atoms.
The achievement lies in making present-day quantum hardware participate in a protein-scale calculation while preserving a route to systematically improved accuracy. The honest constraint sits in the same record: leading classical methods still perform better overall, and the medical value remains upstream of laboratory or clinical validation. This combination is more informative than a simple claim of quantum advantage. It tells research leaders where to look next. Independent groups can test the fragment selection, reproduce resource accounting, compare stronger classical baselines, and ask whether the method changes a real molecular decision.
The economics follow the architecture. More than 100 hours of quantum execution, two supercomputers, and 1.3 billion measurements are substantial research resources. A future production method will need to justify those resources through accuracy or scientific reach unavailable at lower cost.

you.snippet:
A collaboration between Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN, and IBM Quantum has achieved the largest heterogeneous quantum-classical (HQC) electronic-structure calculation to date, simulating protein-ligand complexes exceeding 12,000 atoms. This research utilized 156-qubit IBM Heron r2 processors and leadership supercomputers to significantly advance molecular size and fragment energy accuracy in drug binding simulations.
Detailed in a technical preprint on arXiv, the team paired two 156-qubit IBM Heron r2 processors with three leadership supercomputers to collect 3.0 billion measurement shots across 21,006 circuits, achieving a greater than 40× increase in molecular size and up to a 210× improvement in fragment energy accuracy over previous quantum-embedding benchmarks. Accurately predicting how small-molecule drugs bind to target proteins requires solving the many-electron Schrödinger equation across thousands of solvated atoms, a regime where standard density functional theory approximations can misrank binding affinities and full-system wavefunction methods exceed classical memory limits.
Using a Prefect-based automated workflow controller to orchestrate asynchronous job queues between IBM Quantum Runtime and the ROQUO supercomputer, the pipeline processed 608 million measurement samples in 62.4 hours of wall-clock time without manual intervention.
